title: Slice Internals & Gotchas
summary: A slice is a three-word **header** — a pointer to a backing array, a length, and a capacity — passed by value. Almost every confusing slice bug comes from one fact: multiple slices can share the same backing array. This lesson unpacks aliasing, the `append` reallocation rule, the three-index slice, and the large-array memory leak.

subtopics.title: The slice header is passed by value
subtopics.explanation: A slice value is a 24-byte struct on 64-bit machines: pointer, length, capacity. Passing a slice copies that header; both headers point at the same backing array. So a function can mutate elements (shared array) but cannot change the caller's length (its own header copy). This single fact explains most slice behavior in this topic.

subtopics.title: Slicing aliases, it doesn't copy
subtopics.explanation: b := a[1:3] creates a new header over a's backing array. Writing b[0] can change a[1]. No data is copied. This sharing is the root of most slice surprises, so knowing when you alias versus copy is essential.

subtopics.title: append: in-place vs reallocation
subtopics.explanation: If a slice has spare capacity, append writes into the existing backing array (visible to aliases) and returns a header with larger len. If capacity is exhausted, append allocates a new, larger array, copies, and returns a header pointing there — silently breaking aliasing with the old array. Whether append reallocates decides if your writes stay visible to other slices.

subtopics.title: The three-index slice a[low:high:max]
subtopics.explanation: a[low:high:max] sets capacity to max-low, so a later append on the sub-slice cannot write past max into the shared array — it is forced to reallocate. Use it to hand out a sub-slice that can't clobber the parent's data, the idiomatic defense against append aliasing.

subtopics.title: copy() makes an independent slice
subtopics.explanation: The built-in copy(dst, src) copies min(len(dst), len(src)) elements between two slices and returns the count. Combined with make, it is the idiomatic way to produce a slice that shares no backing array with the source, breaking any aliasing. This is your escape hatch whenever ownership must be clean.

subtopics.title: The large backing-array leak
subtopics.explanation: Re-slicing a small window of a huge array keeps the WHOLE array alive, because the slice header still points into it. To let the big array be garbage-collected, copy the small window into a fresh slice — the reason copy() matters for memory, not just correctness.

foundations.overview: Slices are the workhorse of Go, but they behave in ways that surprise people who treat them like dynamic arrays in other languages. The key is the slice header: a tiny struct (pointer, length, capacity) that is copied by value, while the data it points at is shared. Once you internalize 'the header is copied, the array is shared,' aliasing bugs, append surprises, and memory leaks all become predictable.
foundations.formalDefinition: A slice is a descriptor — a pointer to a backing array, a length, and a capacity — that provides a dynamically-sized view over a contiguous region of that array; multiple slices may reference overlapping regions of the same backing array.
foundations.whyItMatters: Slice aliasing and append semantics are among the most-tested Go interview topics and a leading cause of real production bugs: corrupted shared data, slices that mysteriously don't grow, and memory that won't free.
foundations.mentalModel: Picture a long shelf of boxes (the backing array). A slice is a labeled bracket marking a section: where it starts (pointer), how many boxes are inside (length), and how far the bracket could extend before hitting the shelf's end (capacity). Copying a slice copies the bracket label, not the boxes — two brackets can frame the same boxes.
foundations.runtimePerspective: The header is 24 bytes (pointer + two ints) on 64-bit. append checks len < cap: if room, it writes in place and bumps len; otherwise it calls growslice, which allocates a larger array (growth factor ~2x for small slices, tapering toward ~1.25x for large ones — never rely on the exact factor), copies elements, and returns a header for the new array. The garbage collector keeps a backing array alive as long as any slice header points into it.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Parsing buffers, building response bodies, windowing time-series data, splitting byte streams, and passing sub-slices between pipeline stages.
foundations.businessImpact: Aliasing bugs cause data corruption incidents that are expensive to diagnose; backing-array leaks inflate memory and cloud cost. Knowing the rules prevents both.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Correct slice ownership (who may mutate, who must copy) is a design decision at API boundaries; getting it wrong leaks one request's data into another's.
foundations.performanceImpact: Each capacity overflow is an allocation plus a full copy. Pre-sizing with make([]T, 0, n) turns many O(n) growth copies into one allocation; copying out a small window frees a large array sooner, reducing GC pressure.
commonUseCases: Copying a window out so a large array can be freed

commonMisconceptions.reality: It creates a new header over the SAME backing array; no data is copied until you copy() or append forces a reallocation.

commonMisconceptions.myth: append always grows the caller's slice.
commonMisconceptions.reality: append returns a new header; if you don't assign it back, or if it reallocates, the caller's variable/aliases won't reflect the change.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Re-slicing a big array to a tiny window frees the rest.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The header still points into the big array, keeping ALL of it alive; copy the window out to release the big array.

visualExplorer.title: Anatomy of a slice and its aliases
visualExplorer.caption: Two slices can be different headers over the same backing array. append fills toward cap, then reallocates a new array — silently ending the aliasing.

visualExplorer.title: What append decides each call
visualExplorer.caption: The branch append takes determines whether aliases still see your writes.

steps.name: Check len < cap
steps.detail: append compares the slice's length to its capacity to decide if there is room.

steps.name: Room available
steps.detail: It writes the new element into the existing backing array and returns a header with len+1 — aliases over that array can see the change.

steps.name: No room
steps.detail: It allocates a larger backing array (growth factor implementation-defined) and copies the existing elements.

steps.name: Return new header
steps.detail: The returned header points at the new array; the old array (and any aliases of it) are now disconnected.

steps.name: Assign back
steps.detail: You must write s = append(s, x); otherwise your variable keeps the old, shorter header.

interactiveExamples.title: Aliasing in action: sub-slice writes leak back
interactiveExamples.explanation: b is a window into a's backing array, so writing through b changes a. Then an append that fits within capacity also overwrites a's next element — a classic surprise.

code.code:
package main

import "fmt"

func main() {
	a := []int{1, 2, 3, 4}
	b := a[0:2]            // header over a's array, len 2, cap 4
	b[0] = 99              // writes into the shared array
	fmt.Println(a)         // [99 2 3 4] — a sees b's write
	b = append(b, 100)     // cap allows it -> overwrites a[2] in place
	fmt.Println(a)         // [99 2 100 4] — append clobbered a[2]
	fmt.Println(b)         // [99 2 100]
}

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: stop the sub-slice from clobbering the parent
interactiveExamples.explanation: Use a three-index slice to cap b's capacity so its append is forced to reallocate instead of writing into a. Make a stay [1 2 3 4].

checkpoints.code:
a := []int{1, 2, 3}
b := a[:2]
b = append(b, 99)
fmt.Println(a)
checkpoints.explanation: b has len 2 and cap 3 (shares a's array). append has room, so it writes 99 into the third slot of the shared array — which is a[2]. So a becomes [1 2 99].

checkpoints.prompt: You return sub-slices of a reused parse buffer to callers and they later see corrupted data. What's the safest fix?
options: Copy each window into a fresh slice before returning it
Set the buffer to nil after each call
checkpoints.explanation: Sub-slices alias the reused buffer, so the next parse overwrites earlier results. Copying the window out (e.g. append([]byte(nil), w...)) gives each caller independent data.

checkpoints.prompt: This holds onto far more memory than expected. Why?
options: The returned header still points into huge, keeping the entire huge array alive
checkpoints.explanation: huge[:10] is a header into huge's backing array, so the whole array can't be garbage-collected while the result is referenced. Copy out: out := make([]byte, 10); copy(out, huge[:10]); return out.

checkpoints.prompt: Hand out the first two elements of buf so the caller's append cannot overwrite buf[2].
checkpoints.explanation: buf[0:2:2] sets length 2 and capacity 2, so any append on head must reallocate rather than write into buf[2]. buf[0:2] leaves spare capacity and would clobber buf's data on append.

codeLab.title: Remove an index without leaking or corrupting
codeLab.instructions: Implement `Remove(s []int, i int) []int` that returns s with the element at index i removed, preserving order. Mutating s's backing array is allowed (in-place shift), but the returned slice must have the correct length. Assume 0 <= i < len(s).
hints: copy(s[i:], s[i+1:]) shifts everything after i down by one slot.
Return s[:len(s)-1] to drop the duplicated last element.
This reuses the backing array; if callers must not see mutation, have them pass a copy.

debuggingLab.title: Appending to a sub-slice corrupts a sibling
debuggingLab.symptom: After building two sub-slices from the same source and appending to one, the other slice's data is unexpectedly changed.

brokenCode.code:
base := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
left := base[0:2]   // len 2, cap 5
right := base[2:4]  // len 2, cap 3
left = append(left, 99) // writes into base[2] -> corrupts right!
fmt.Println(right)  // [99 4] instead of [3 4]

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: left has spare capacity in base's backing array, so append(left, 99) writes into base[2], which is right[0]. left and right alias overlapping regions of one array, so one's append silently mutates the other.
commonMistakes: Assuming sub-slices are independent of their source.
Appending to a sub-slice that still has shared capacity.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Cap each sub-slice's capacity with a three-index slice so an append must reallocate instead of writing into shared memory.

solution.code:
base := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
left := base[0:2:2]  // cap capped at 2
right := base[2:4:4] // cap capped at 4
left = append(left, 99) // cap exhausted -> reallocates, base untouched
fmt.Println(right)   // [3 4]

theory.question: Describe the slice header and explain why a function can mutate a slice's elements but not extend the caller's slice.
theory.directAnswer: A slice header is three words: a pointer to a backing array, a length, and a capacity. When you pass a slice, the header is copied by value but the pointer still points at the same backing array — so the function can mutate elements (shared memory). It cannot extend the caller's slice because append returns a new header; the function's local header copy gets the new length/pointer, but the caller's header is unchanged unless you return and reassign it.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The (pointer, length, capacity) descriptor that is a slice value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To give a cheap, copyable view over a shared, growable array.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Copying the header shares the array; element writes go to shared memory, but length lives only in the local header copy.

theory.whyImportant: This single fact explains both mutation-through-functions and the must-reassign-append rule — a core interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: func normalize(v []float64) mutates values in place for the caller, but a func that grows the slice must return it.

followUps.question: How big is the header on a 64-bit machine?
followUps.answer: 24 bytes: an 8-byte pointer plus two 8-byte ints.

followUps.question: How do you let a function extend the caller's slice?
followUps.answer: Return the result and have the caller reassign (s = grow(s)), or pass a *[]T pointer.

theory.question: What does the three-index slice expression s[low:high:max] do and when would you use it?
theory.directAnswer: It produces a slice with length high-low and capacity max-low (instead of defaulting capacity to the end of the backing array). You use it to hand out a sub-slice whose append is guaranteed to reallocate rather than write past `max` into the parent's backing array — protecting shared data from aliasing-via-append bugs.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A full slice expression that explicitly sets the resulting capacity.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To cap capacity so appends can't reach into memory the sub-slice shouldn't own.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: With cap == len, the next append finds no room and allocates a fresh array, breaking the alias safely.

theory.whyImportant: It's the idiomatic defense against sub-slice append corruption, and a senior-level slice question.
theory.realWorldExample: Returning header := buf[0:n:n] from a parser so the caller can append without clobbering the rest of buf.

followUps.question: What must be true about low, high, max?
followUps.answer: low <= high <= max <= cap(original); otherwise it panics at runtime / fails to compile for constants.

theory.question: Explain append's growth mechanics: when does it write in place versus reallocate, what growth factor does it use, and why must you always write s = append(s, x)?
theory.directAnswer: append checks len < cap. If there is spare capacity it writes the element into the existing backing array in place and returns a header with len+1 pointing at the same array. If capacity is exhausted, the runtime calls growslice, which allocates a new, larger backing array, copies the existing elements over, and returns a header pointing at the new array — the old array is left behind. The growth factor is roughly 2x for small slices, tapering toward ~1.25x for large ones (never rely on the exact number). You must reassign s = append(s, x) because append returns a header by value: on reallocation the pointer and capacity change, and even without reallocation the length changes, so if you discard the return value your variable keeps the old, shorter header. Pre-sizing with make([]T, 0, n) reserves capacity up front so a known number of appends never reallocate.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The in-place-vs-reallocate decision append makes each call, plus the amortized growth strategy.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Amortized doubling gives O(1) amortized append while bounding wasted memory; returning a header keeps slices value-typed and cheap to pass.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: len < cap -> write in place, bump len; len == cap -> growslice allocates ~2x (tapering to ~1.25x), copies, returns a new header. The caller must capture that header.

theory.whyImportant: Misunderstanding this causes both 'my append didn't stick' bugs and hidden O(n^2) growth from repeated reallocation in loops.
theory.realWorldExample: Building a 1M-element slice with no pre-size triggers ~20 reallocations and copies; make([]T, 0, 1_000_000) does it in a single allocation.

followUps.question: Why is the growth factor not exactly 2x for large slices?
followUps.answer: Doubling huge slices wastes too much memory, so the runtime tapers toward ~1.25x for large ones to trade a bit more copying for less waste.

followUps.question: Does append ever shrink capacity?
followUps.answer: No — append only grows or reuses capacity; to release capacity you must allocate a new, smaller slice and copy.

theory.question: Is a slice safe to use concurrently across goroutines? Distinguish concurrent reads, concurrent writes to distinct indices, and concurrent append.
theory.directAnswer: A slice header carries no synchronization, so it is not inherently safe for concurrent use. Concurrent reads of an unchanging slice are fine. Concurrent writes to the SAME index are a data race and must be synchronized. Writes to DISJOINT index ranges of the same backing array are safe without a lock as long as the ranges never overlap and no one is appending — this is the standard pattern for parallelizing work over a pre-allocated result slice (each goroutine owns a partition). Concurrent append to the same slice is always a race: each append reads and mutates the shared len (and may reallocate), so two goroutines appending corrupt the header and the array; you must lock, or have each goroutine append to its own slice and merge afterward.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The concurrency guarantees (and lack thereof) of slices and their backing arrays.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Slices are a low-level view with no built-in locking, matching Go's 'share memory by communicating' philosophy.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Distinct memory locations can be written concurrently safely; shared locations (same index, or the shared length field that append mutates) require synchronization to avoid a race.

theory.whyImportant: The 'partition disjoint ranges vs lock vs concurrent-append-is-a-race' distinction is a precise concurrency question that separates careful engineers.
theory.realWorldExample: A worker pool computing results into out[i] where each worker owns a fixed range of i needs no lock; but if workers each append to a shared results slice they race and must instead append to per-worker slices merged at the end.

followUps.question: How would the race detector view disjoint-index writes?
followUps.answer: It reports no race because the goroutines touch different memory addresses; the danger is only if ranges overlap or someone appends/reslices concurrently.

followUps.question: What's the idiomatic alternative to locking around append?
followUps.answer: Give each goroutine its own slice (or a channel), then concatenate/collect the results after all workers finish — no shared mutation.

scenario.question: A service reads small records by slicing a large network buffer and storing the sub-slices in a cache. Memory grows far beyond the cached data size. Diagnose and fix.
scenario.directAnswer: Each cached sub-slice is a header into the large buffer's backing array, so the entire buffer stays alive as long as any sub-slice is cached — the GC can't free it. Fix it by copying each record out into a right-sized slice (out := make([]byte, len(rec)); copy(out, rec)) before caching, so the big buffers can be collected.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A backing-array leak caused by retaining sub-slices of large buffers.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A slice keeps its whole backing array reachable, regardless of how small the window is.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: GC reachability follows the header's pointer to the full array; copying out removes that reference.

scenario.whyImportant: This is a common, costly real-world memory leak in network and parsing code.
scenario.realWorldExample: Caching HTTP header values as sub-slices of the connection's read buffer pinned megabytes per connection.

followUps.question: How would you confirm the diagnosis?
followUps.answer: A heap profile (pprof) shows large []byte backing arrays retained by the cache entries.

scenario.question: A high-throughput parser reuses a pooled []byte read buffer across requests and returns sub-slices of it (e.g. a parsed token) to the caller, which stores them. Occasionally request A's response contains bytes from request B. Diagnose the bug and fix it.
scenario.directAnswer: The returned tokens are sub-slices aliasing the pooled buffer's backing array. When the buffer is reused (or reset via sync.Pool) for the next request, its bytes are overwritten in place — and because the previous caller retained a sub-slice into that same array, it now sees the new request's bytes. This is both a correctness bug and a security issue: one request's data leaks into another's. Fix it by copying each retained window OUT of the shared buffer before returning: out := make([]byte, len(tok)); copy(out, tok) (or append([]byte(nil), tok...)). If you must hand out a live sub-slice, use a three-index slice tok := buf[i:j:j] so the caller's append can't reach into the rest of the buffer — but copying is the safe default when the caller retains the data. Establish an ownership rule at the API boundary: returned slices that alias a reused buffer must be documented as valid only until the next parse, or copied.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A cross-request data leak from aliasing a reused/pooled backing array.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A slice keeps pointing into whatever backing array it was cut from; reusing that array silently mutates every retained sub-slice.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The pool returns the same []byte; the parser writes new bytes into it; retained sub-slices, being windows into that array, now read the new bytes.

scenario.whyImportant: This is a real, dangerous class of bug (correctness + security) in parsers and network servers and a strong senior scenario question.
scenario.realWorldExample: An HTTP parser returning header values as sub-slices of the connection read buffer served one connection's cookie to another after the buffer was reused.

followUps.question: When is three-indexing enough instead of copying?
followUps.answer: Three-indexing (buf[i:j:j]) only protects against append clobbering neighbors; it does NOT stop the leak if the buffer itself is reused while the caller still holds the slice — for retention you must copy.

followUps.question: How would you detect this in review?
followUps.answer: Flag any function that returns a sub-slice of a buffer obtained from sync.Pool or reused across calls; require a copy or an explicit 'valid until next call' contract.

systemDesign.question: Design a high-throughput byte-buffer strategy for a parser or network server that minimizes allocations and GC pressure while staying correct. Cover buffer reuse, pre-sizing, copying windows, and ownership rules.
systemDesign.directAnswer: Use a sync.Pool of []byte read buffers so per-request buffers are recycled instead of freshly allocated, resetting each to len 0 (keeping capacity) on Put. Pre-size buffers with make([]byte, 0, n) to a typical request size so appends rarely grow. While parsing, work on sub-slices (windows) of the pooled buffer for zero-copy speed — but the moment a value must OUTLIVE the current request (cached, queued, returned to a handler that retains it), copy that small window into a right-sized slice so the large pooled buffer can be returned and reused. Copying small windows out also breaks the large-backing-array leak: a 4-byte token should not pin a 64KB buffer. Define ownership rules at every API boundary: functions either (a) return copies the caller owns, or (b) return aliases explicitly documented as valid only until the buffer is reused. Use three-index slices when handing out windows a caller might append to. Benchmark and profile with pprof inuse_space to confirm buffers are freed and not pinned.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A memory-management policy combining pooling, pre-sizing, selective copying, and explicit ownership.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To sustain high throughput without per-request allocations while avoiding aliasing leaks and cross-request data corruption.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: sync.Pool amortizes allocation; pre-sizing avoids growslice; copying windows before retention frees the big buffer and prevents leaks; ownership contracts prevent aliasing bugs.

systemDesign.whyImportant: It ties together every slice-internals concept into a realistic performance/correctness design that senior interviews love.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: net/http and high-performance parsers pool read buffers and copy header/body windows out before handing them to user code.

followUps.question: What's the risk of putting a grown buffer back in the pool?
followUps.answer: If requests occasionally balloon a buffer, pooling the huge one pins memory; cap the size you return to the pool (discard oversized buffers) to avoid retaining giant arrays.

followUps.question: How do you decide zero-copy vs copy?
followUps.answer: Zero-copy (sub-slice) for data consumed before the buffer is reused; copy for anything retained beyond the current request — retention lifetime is the deciding factor.

coding.question: Implement `func Chunk[T any](s []T, size int) [][]T` that splits s into consecutive chunks of at most `size` elements (the last chunk may be shorter). Return nil when size <= 0, and handle empty input.
coding.thoughtProcess: First guard the invalid case: size <= 0 has no meaningful chunk size, so return nil. For empty (but non-nil-required) input the loop simply never runs and we return an empty result. I pre-size the outer slice to the exact number of chunks, ceil(len/size), to avoid reallocation. Then I step i by size and slice s[i:end] where end is min(i+size, len(s)) so the final chunk is naturally shorter. I return sub-slices of s (aliasing) which is the idiomatic zero-copy behavior; callers who mutate should copy — I'd note that rather than defensively copy.
coding.lineByLine: We return nil immediately for size <= 0. We compute the number of chunks as ceil(n/size) via (n+size-1)/size and pre-allocate the outer slice to that capacity so append never reallocates. The loop advances i in steps of size; end is i+size clamped to n so the last chunk is shorter when n isn't a multiple of size. Each chunk is s[i:end], a window into s's backing array (zero-copy). For empty input the loop body never executes and we return an empty [][]T.
coding.timeComplexity: O(len(s)/size) chunk operations — effectively O(n) work to produce headers (no element copying).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n/size) for the outer slice of chunk headers; chunks alias s, so no per-element copy.

followUps.question: Why do the chunks share s's backing array, and when is that a problem?
followUps.answer: s[i:end] is a window, not a copy; mutating a chunk mutates s. If callers need independent chunks, copy each: c := append([]T(nil), s[i:end]...).

followUps.question: What does Chunk return for empty input versus size <= 0?
followUps.answer: For empty input it returns an empty (non-nil, zero-length) [][]T because the loop never runs; for size <= 0 it explicitly returns nil.

coding.question: Implement `func Clone(s []int) []int` that returns an independent copy with no shared backing array, and handles nil correctly.
coding.thoughtProcess: I must not share the backing array, so I allocate a fresh slice of the same length and copy. For nil input I should return nil (not an empty non-nil slice) to preserve nil semantics. make + copy is the idiomatic, allocation-minimal approach.
coding.lineByLine: We return nil for nil input so callers can distinguish 'no slice' from 'empty slice'. Otherwise we allocate a new array sized to len(s) and copy the elements; the returned slice shares nothing with s, so later mutations to either are independent.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the new backing array.

followUps.question: How does the standard library do this generically?
followUps.answer: slices.Clone[S ~[]E, E any](s S) S does exactly this for any element type.

followUps.question: Why not return s[:] for a copy?
followUps.answer: s[:] is the same backing array — not independent; mutations would alias the original.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Define ownership at API boundaries: document whether a returned slice may be retained/mutated by the caller. Defensively copy untrusted or reused-buffer slices before storing them, and use s[i:j:j] when handing out windows that callers might append to.
productionDeepDive.performance: Pre-size with make([]T, 0, n) in hot loops to avoid repeated growslice allocations and copies. Reuse buffers via sync.Pool for high-throughput parsing, and copy small windows out of large buffers to let the big arrays free promptly.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: A slice header is not safe for concurrent writes to the same indices. Partition disjoint index ranges per goroutine, or guard shared slices with a mutex; concurrent append to the same slice is a data race.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always write s = append(s, x). Be wary of aliasing when slicing reused buffers; a single shared backing array can leak one request's bytes into another's response — a correctness and security hazard.
productionDeepDive.observability: Watch pprof alloc_space for unexpected slice growth and inuse_space for retained large backing arrays (the leak signature). Sudden allocation spikes in a loop usually mean a missing pre-size.
productionDeepDive.security: Never return sub-slices of buffers that held other requests' data without copying; aliasing can leak cross-request bytes. Cap handed-out windows with three-index slices so callers cannot read/overwrite neighboring data via append.

caseStudies.problem: GC pressure from per-record slice growth and pinned large read buffers.
caseStudies.solution: Pre-sized buffers, sync.Pool reuse, and copying small windows out of large buffers.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More explicit memory management for big allocation and latency savings.
caseStudies.lessons: Understanding len/cap and backing-array reachability turns hidden O(n) copies and leaks into controlled, single allocations.

caseStudies.problem: Caching sub-slices of large buffers pinned far more memory than the cached data.
caseStudies.solution: Copy each value into a right-sized slice before caching.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: One copy per cached item vs. holding entire backing arrays alive.
caseStudies.lessons: A slice keeps its whole array reachable — copy windows out when retaining them.

keyTakeaways: A slice is a 24-byte header (pointer, length, capacity) passed by value; the header is copied but the backing array is shared.
Slicing aliases the same array — writes and capacity-fitting appends through one slice can change another; always assign s = append(s, x).
Use the three-index slice s[i:j:j] to cap capacity so a handed-out sub-slice's append reallocates instead of clobbering shared data.
Retaining a sub-slice of a large array keeps the whole array alive — copy the window out (make + copy) to free the big backing array.
